extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate/graduate students and researchers in theoretical mechanics, calculus of variations, and history of mathematical physics
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation and development of isoperimetric and variational problems in mechanics: historical methods (Fermat, Bernoulli, Euler, Lagrange, Jellett), classification of problems, and the derivation of the variational (Euler–Lagrange) conditions and boundary terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of formal development
rubrics_metrics.description: To put in a clear compendious form, or system, the facts to be reproduced, so that each can be reached and mentally pictured with the least intellectual effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In formal development strive for greatest possible uniformity and rules easy of acquisition; combine with deductive development though not sharply separated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of tangents for maxima and minima
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the maximum or minimum values of a quantity depending on another, seek the parallel tangents of its curve—at extrema the tangents are generally parallel to the axis of abscissas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete example: maximize product x(a−x) by regarding it as y(x) and noting that an infinitesimal variation produces no first-order change; algebraic translation yields the condition that leads to differential calculus (derivative zero).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fermat's principle (least time)
rubrics_metrics.description: Light emitted from A and refracted at M to B travels by the path for which the time is a minimum; neighboring infinitely near paths take the same time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to refraction law v1 sin α = v2 sin β (index of refraction n = v1/v2). Hero's law of reflection is a special case. Use perpendicular projections and velocity differences to derive condition for extremal time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Huygens' extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Fermat's idea applies not only to rectilinear but also to curvilinear motions of light in media with continuously varying velocity; Fermat's law still obtains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat velocity as a continuous function of position; consider variational principle of minimal time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of least potential / virtual velocities in mechanics
rubrics_metrics.description: A freely suspended chain assumes the form for which its centre of gravity lies lowest; mechanical motions display maximal or minimal properties analogous to optical least-time principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use principle of virtual velocities to motivate variational treatment of mechanical problems (e.g., catenary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brachistochrone solution via optical analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: The curve of quickest descent between two points in a vertical plane (brachistochrone) is a cycloid; John Bernoulli solved it by treating the falling body's path as analogous to a light ray in a layered medium where v varies with depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume v = √(2gh) (velocity as function of vertical drop), derive differential equation dy/dx = expression leading to cycloid; construct specific cycloid by similarity/scaling to pass through given endpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: James Bernoulli's three principles for isoperimetric problems
rubrics_metrics.description: (1) If a curve has a certain property of maximum or minimum, every portion or element of the curve has the same property. (2) The quantity to be extremized is constant for infinitely contiguous curves (analogy to ordinary maxima/minima). (3) For the brachistochrone assume v = √(2gh).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these principles to deduce angle/velocity sine relations for small elements; note that James's geometrical method yields general procedure for selecting extremal curve among infinitely many.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of local-element principle in resisting media
rubrics_metrics.description: James Bernoulli's assumption that if the whole curve is brachistochronous every element is also brachistochronous does not hold in resisting media, because velocity in an element can depend on the preceding path.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases where local velocity depends on entire preceding path, a more detailed nonlocal treatment is required; do not assume elementwise extremality universally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler's classification of isoperimetric problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide problems into classes: (1) Of all curves find one for which property A is extremal. (2) Of all curves possessing property A find one for which B is extremal. (3) Of all curves possessing A and B find one for which C is extremal, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: shortest curve through two points (class 1); curve through two points of given length making area maximal (class 2); show how higher-class problems reduce to first-class by combining functionals with constants (A + mB).

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting degrees of variation
rubrics_metrics.description: The solution of problems of differing classes requires varying different numbers of elements: first class requires variation of two elements (or one point), second class three elements (two points), third class four elements, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This counting explains why additional boundary conditions/arbitrary constants appear; it indicates how many independent variations are necessary to capture constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of commutability / mutuality
rubrics_metrics.description: Solving a higher-class isoperimetric problem implicitly solves its converse forms; e.g., a circle both maximizes area among curves of given length and minimizes length among curves enclosing given area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use algebraic combination (A + mB) to turn constrained extremum into an unconstrained extremum over one functional, sweeping constants (Lagrange multipliers idea).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lagrange's variational idea (increments of form vs independent variable)
rubrics_metrics.description: Increments which functions receive due to change in their form are analogous to increments from change in independent variables; denote variations (change of form) by d (variation symbol) and differentials (change in independent variables) by d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analogy lets one write immediately the equations solving maxima/minima of functionals; Lagrange did not provide rigorous verification but showed powerful applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jellett's clarification of variation/differential
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantities split into constant and variable; variable subdivided into independent and dependent (functions). For an indeterminate form y = φ(x), the change in y can be due to dx (differential dy) or due to change of form φ→φ+δφ (variation δy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat an integral (like arc length) as a determinate function of an indeterminate function; formulate variation δU by substituting y+δy and expand to first order to get variation expression. This clarifies the logical status of variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: General variational problem setup (functionals and DU=0)
rubrics_metrics.description: For U = ∫ F(x,y,y',...,y^(n)) dx the total change DU equals contributions from changes of limits plus the variation due to form change; extremum imposes DU = 0, leading after integration by parts to boundary terms and an integral term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform successive integration by parts to remove higher-order δ(y^(k)) terms, collect boundary terms (depend on limit variations) and interior integral. Necessary conditions: boundary term expressions equal zero and integrand multiplying arbitrary δy must vanish (Euler–Lagrange conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration by parts to eliminate higher derivatives in variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the formula ∫ u dv = uv − ∫ v du repeatedly so that the variation expression contains only δy under the integral sign, moving derivatives onto multiplying coefficients and producing boundary terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedure yields the standard form where the integrand is a linear combination of δy; then argue that since δy is arbitrary, the coefficient (the Euler–Lagrange expression) must be zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boundary (limit) conditions and transversality
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms arising from integration by parts split into (i) terms depending solely on variation of the limits, (ii) terms depending on changes of form at the limiting values of x, and (iii) terms depending on the general form change. For DU = 0 these boundary contributions must vanish: a_i − a_0 = 0 and the integrand (Euler expression) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boundary conditions determine arbitrary constants in the general solution; when limits are fixed many boundary terms vanish, otherwise transversality or natural boundary conditions apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaninglessness of absolute extrema without constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding an absolute maximum or minimum without collateral conditions is meaningless—extrema are defined relative to a set of admissible functions sharing given constraints (e.g., passing through fixed points).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always specify constraints (fixed points, fixed length, enclosed area, etc.) when posing variational problems; classify problem according to which quantities are held fixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euler–Lagrange equation as necessary condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The differential equation obtained (denoted equation (3) in the text) that the extremal function y = φ(x) must satisfy is the Euler–Lagrange equation; its general solution contains arbitrary constants fixed by boundary conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equation arises from setting the coefficient of arbitrary δy under the integral to zero. Use it to determine the extremal form up to constants determined by limit conditions.
